text: Everything so far has run on a single Docker host. Kubernetes is what you reach for when one host isn't enough, and the first thing to understand about a cluster is that it's two kinds of machine. Control plane nodes decide what should be running. Worker nodes actually run it. That split explains almost everything else in this chapter.

The control plane is four components, each with one job. kube-apiserver is the front door — every kubectl command, every controller, every kubelet report goes through it as a REST call. etcd is the cluster's database, the single source of truth for every object's state. kube-scheduler decides which node a new pod should land on. And kube-controller-manager runs the reconciliation loops that make Kubernetes self-healing, constantly comparing desired state to observed state and closing the gap.

Run kubectl get nodes against a real cluster and the split is visible immediately. On a managed cluster like AKS or EKS, the cloud provider hides the control plane entirely — you'll only ever see worker nodes listed here, each one ready to run your application's containers.

On a self-managed cluster, though, you can watch the control plane itself as ordinary pods in the kube-system namespace — etcd, the API server, the controller manager, and the scheduler, each one a container being supervised by a kubelet, just like any application you'd deploy.

Every worker node runs three things. kubelet watches the API server for pods assigned to its own node and makes sure their containers are actually running. The container runtime — containerd, on virtually every modern cluster — is what actually pulls images and starts containers, through a standard interface called the CRI. And kube-proxy keeps each node's network rules in sync so Services can route traffic to the right pods.

Decide, then execute — that's the whole architecture. Next lesson builds on top of it: the object hierarchy that turns one scheduling decision into a self-healing set of replicas, and why Kubernetes uses three layered objects instead of just one.
